review.rationale: Primary empirical evidence directly evaluating the specified exposure (baseline NLR >= 3 vs < 3) and outcome (progression-free survival) in patients with non-small cell lung cancer is provided by MED:40941007. In that retrospective cohort of 180 NSCLC patients, baseline NLR >= 3 was significantly associated with an increased hazard of progression (HR 1.60, 95% CI 1.10-2.32, p = 0.014), indicating shorter PFS (negative mean log-PFS contrast). This directional relationship is further corroborated across metastatic and general NSCLC cohorts receiving immune therapies by meta-analysis MED:42180874.

realism.rationale: Elevated baseline neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR >= 3) is a thoroughly established adverse prognostic factor across all stages of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Multiple real-world cohorts and meta-analyses (including MED:41901549, MED:40941007, and MED:42180874) demonstrate that NLR >= 3 is consistently associated with significantly shorter progression-free survival (PFS) across various treatment modalities (chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapies, chemoradiation, and surgical resection). The directional effect of -1 for log_pfs_months correctly reflects this inferior outcome, and the 'expected' category is fully supported.
realism.counterexample_search: Evaluated potential strata allowed by empty eligibility, including resectable early-stage NSCLC, oncogenic driver-mutated NSCLC (EGFR/ALK/KRAS), and metastatic disease treated with chemo-immunotherapy or targeted agents. In none of these settings is high baseline systemic inflammation (NLR >= 3) known or expected to confer a favorable PFS outcome; the adverse prognostic association transports consistently across all major subgroups.

realism.rationale: In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), Stage IV (metastatic disease) universally portends an inferior prognosis compared to earlier stages (Stages I-III). Earlier-stage patients are candidates for curative-intent modalities (surgical resection, definitive stereotactic body radiation, or concurrent chemoradiotherapy) yielding prolonged disease-free or progression-free intervals and substantial cure fractions. In contrast, Stage IV disease is systemic and typically incurable, with median progression-free survival (PFS) governed by the duration of response to systemic palliative therapy. Multivariable survival analyses demonstrate that Stage IV disease is an independent unfavorable prognostic factor for PFS and survival across histologic and molecular subgroups.
realism.counterexample_search: Searched for any patient stratum permitted by the unselected cohort eligibility where Stage IV patients would experience longer progression-free survival than earlier-stage (Stage I-III) patients. Across all molecular subtypes (EGFR, KRAS, ALK, or driver-negative), histologic classes (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma), and performance status categories, earlier-stage patients consistently exhibit longer recurrence-free/progression-free survival than metastatic (Stage IV) patients due to the efficacy of curative-intent local therapies and lower overall tumor burden. No counterexample stratum exists where metastatic stage IV NSCLC systematically outperforms early-stage disease in PFS.

review.rationale: Direct primary empirical evidence supports that elevated baseline C-reactive protein (CRP >= 10 mg/L vs < 10 mg/L) is significantly associated with shorter progression-free survival (PFS) in patients with NSCLC. In a large cohort of 1,339 lung cancer patients (82.7% NSCLC), MED:42291343 showed that CRP >= 10 mg/L independently predicted shorter PFS (adjusted HR = 1.28, 95% CI: 1.14-1.43, p < 0.001) and in the NSCLC subgroup analysis median PFS was significantly shorter (9.0 vs 13.0 months, p < 0.001). MED:41976392 evaluated metastatic NSCLC patients treated with nivolumab and also found elevated CRP (> 10 mg/L vs <= 10 mg/L) was independently associated with shorter PFS (multivariable HR = 2.14, 95% CI: 1.10-4.17, p = 0.023).

realism.rationale: Elevated baseline C-reactive protein (CRP >= 10 mg/L) is a well-established negative prognostic biomarker indicating systemic inflammation and poor clinical outcomes across non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). In a large cohort of lung cancer patients (MED:42291343), baseline CRP >= 10 mg/L independently predicted significantly shorter progression-free survival (multivariate HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.14-1.43, p < 0.001; median PFS 9.0 vs 13.0 months in NSCLC). A meta-analysis in NSCLC (MED:39478006) confirmed elevated CRP is significantly associated with reduced PFS (HR 1.50, 95% CI 1.33-1.67, p < 0.001), and multicenter real-world cohorts (MED:41976392) also identify elevated CRP as independently associated with inferior PFS. The negative direction on log_pfs_months (direction: -1) directly reflects shorter PFS in the exposed group (crp_mg_l_ge_10 = 1).
realism.counterexample_search: Evaluated whether any patient subpopulation within NSCLC (by histology, oncogenic driver mutation status, stage, or systemic therapy regimen) exhibits longer PFS with elevated baseline CRP >= 10 mg/L. Across all evaluated clinical subgroups, systemic inflammation indicated by CRP >= 10 mg/L is consistently associated with worse or neutral disease control and survival, with no evidence of a paradoxical protective effect.

candidate.statement: Poor performance status (ECOG PS >= 2) is associated with significantly shorter progression-free survival compared to good performance status (ECOG PS < 2) in NSCLC.
queries: "ECOG performance status" "progression-free survival" advanced NSCLC prognostic

review.rationale: Multiple primary empirical studies in NSCLC evaluate the contrast of ECOG PS >= 2 versus ECOG PS < 2 on progression-free survival (PFS). Specifically, MED:42187584 shows that in advanced NSCLC patients, ECOG performance status 2 versus 0-1 was independently associated with significantly inferior PFS (multivariable HR 3.09, 95% CI 1.74-5.48, p < 0.001). MED:42645345 similarly documents that ECOG performance status >= 2 versus 0-1 was independently associated with worse PFS (multivariable HR 3.63, p = 0.004). MED:42346239 also reports in NSCLC patients that ECOG PS >= 2 is associated with significantly shorter PFS (multivariable HR 1.84, 95% CI 1.42-2.38, p < 0.001). Therefore, poor performance status (ECOG PS >= 2) is empirically supported as being associated with shorter PFS (negative log PFS, direction -1).

realism.rationale: Poor performance status (ECOG PS >= 2 vs 0-1) is a universally established adverse prognostic factor in non-small cell lung cancer, consistently associated with significantly shorter progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival across all histologies, stages, driver-mutation subsets, and therapeutic modalities (including chemotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and targeted therapies such as osimertinib). The unconstrained cohort scope is fully defensible.
realism.counterexample_search: Evaluated potential counterexample subgroups, including patients with oncogenic driver alterations (e.g., EGFR-mutant NSCLC on osimertinib), squamous vs non-squamous histologies, high vs low PD-L1 expression, and various lines of systemic therapy. Across all examined clinical subsets in the retrieved evidence and standard oncology literature, ECOG PS >= 2 is consistently an independent adverse prognostic factor for PFS (e.g., HR > 1.8-3.6 for progression/death compared to PS 0-1), with no identifiable stratum where poor performance status confers prolonged PFS.

queries: BRCA2 mutant versus wild-type NSCLC PFS

review.rationale: The candidate proposes a neutral hypothesis evaluating the association between BRCA2 mutation status and progression-free survival (log_pfs_months) in unselected NSCLC within a newly constructed exploratory subgroup defined by research signatures A and B. In unselected NSCLC broad cohorts, BRCA2 mutation does not have an established directional prognostic association with PFS (unlike driver oncogenes such as EGFR or classic TSGs like STK11/KEAP1). While studies look at DDR alterations in specific treatment contexts (e.g., EGFR-TKIs or platinum chemotherapy), there is no established standalone or inherited directional PFS association for BRCA2 mutation across unselected NSCLC. Therefore, broader_direction is none, supporting the neutral candidate.
review.neutrality_rationale: In unselected NSCLC, BRCA2 mutation status has no established, consistent prognostic association with progression-free survival. The exploratory subgrouping based on research signatures A and B does not inherit any established directional effect from the parent exposure-outcome comparison.

realism.rationale: In non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), BRCA2 mutations occur at a low frequency (typically 2-5%) and do not have an established, consistent directional prognostic association with progression-free survival (PFS) in an unselected, general NSCLC population. Although some reports suggest homologous recombination deficiency or DNA damage response (DDR) gene alterations may confer increased sensitivity to platinum-based chemotherapies (MED:40386740), other studies show unfavorable or neutral outcomes under targeted therapies or mixed regimens (MED:42092972), and PARP inhibitors remain unapproved as standard-of-care in unselected NSCLC (MED:41772736). As the research signatures A and B are constructed standardized scores with no assigned directional biology, no established directional expectation is inherited from the parent population. Therefore, classifying this contrast as neutral is defensible.
realism.counterexample_search: Considered whether specific subgroups within unselected NSCLC (such as those receiving platinum doublet chemotherapy or EGFR-TKIs) have established directional effects that would violate neutral status across the entire cohort. However, across an unselected NSCLC cohort receiving heterogeneous standard therapies, BRCA2 mutation has no consensus prognostic impact on PFS, confirming the neutral classification.

realism.rationale: The candidate hypothesis evaluates the association between synthetic research marker D positivity and progression-free survival (log_pfs_months) within an exploratory subgroup defined by research signature A >= 0.0 and research signature C <= 0.5. Per the benchmark design specifications, research marker D and research signatures A and C are explicitly constructed features with no assigned biological identity or known directional role. Consequently, there is no inherited directional expectation from the published literature across any clinical or molecular subset in NSCLC. Classifying this hypothesis as neutral is valid.
realism.counterexample_search: Evaluated whether any specific patient subset within NSCLC (e.g., defined by EGFR/KRAS/ALK driver alterations, stage, or specific therapy lines) would have an established biological or clinical expectation regarding research marker D or the signature-defined subgroup. Because research marker D and signatures A and C are purely synthetic constructs without biological analogs or parent biomarkers, no patient stratum carries an inherited directional expectation.

assessment.rationale: The DGP is scientifically valid and internally consistent: (1) Expected components (baseline NLR >= 3, stage IV disease, and CRP >= 10 mg/L) are fully supported by the reviewed clinical literature as adverse prognostic factors across the broad NSCLC population without requiring narrower eligibility restrictions; (2) The only discordant term in the specification is ECOG PS >= 2, which is explicitly designated with category 'surprising'; (3) Hypotheses evaluate distinct clinical, molecular, and synthetic assay exposures without redundant overall/subgroup targets; (4) Neutral discoveries (BRCA2 mutation and synthetic research marker D within exploratory research signature subgroups) do not inherit established directional expectations in unselected NSCLC; and (5) The outcome scale of log_pfs_months with baseline intercept 2.5 (approx. 12.2 months) and effect sizes of 0.45 log units (hazard ratio approx. 1.57) aligns well with empirical NSCLC survival dynamics.
